title: Accusative Case
definition: The accusative case (Akkusativ) is commonly used for the direct object—the person or thing directly affected by an action. In the basic nominative-to-accusative article change, masculine der/ein changes to den/einen; feminine die/eine and neuter das/ein stay the same. Plural definite die also stays die.

rules.title: Find the direct object
rules.explanation: Ask wen? (whom?) or was? (what?) after the verb to help identify the direct object.

rules.title: Definite articles in the accusative
rules.explanation: Only the masculine definite article changes in this basic pattern: der → den. Feminine, neuter, and plural articles stay the same.

rules.title: Indefinite articles in the accusative
rules.explanation: For ein-words, masculine ein changes to einen. Feminine eine and neuter ein remain unchanged.

rules.title: Possessive articles and kein in the accusative
rules.explanation: Possessive articles and kein follow the same basic ending pattern as ein: masculine gets -en, while feminine and neuter singular forms remain unchanged. In plural, keine is used.

rules.title: Common verbs followed by the accusative
rules.explanation: Many everyday verbs take a direct object in the accusative. Learn these verbs with example sentences.

examples.note: Ich habe einen Bruder. — I have a brother.
Ich sehe den Bus. — I see the bus.
Sie kauft einen Apfel. — She buys an apple.
Wir brauchen einen Tisch. — We need a table.
Ich finde den Film gut. — I think the film is good.
Er isst einen Apfel. — He eats an apple.

rules.title: Accusative pronouns
rules.explanation: Some personal pronouns also change in the accusative. Important A1 forms are ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, wir → uns, and ihr → euch.

rules.title: Common accusative prepositions
rules.explanation: These common prepositions require the accusative: durch, für, gegen, ohne, and um. Learn them with a short phrase.

article_changes.example: Der Mann kommt. Ich sehe den Mann.
Die Frau kommt. Ich sehe die Frau.
Das Kind kommt. Ich sehe das Kind.
Die Kinder kommen. Ich sehe die Kinder.

common_mistakes.explanation: Mann is masculine and is the direct object, so der changes to den.
Masculine ein changes to einen in the accusative.
Feminine die does not change in the accusative.
The accusative pronoun for ich is mich.

mastery_goal: You can identify a direct object, use den/einen for masculine accusative nouns, keep feminine and neuter articles correct, and use common accusative pronouns and prepositions in basic A1 sentences.
